teaser: A teenage girl, a duke's secret, and an animal that was not there at first.
review_notes:
Leonardo's letter to Ludovico Sforza listing military skills and mentioning painting at the end: standard account (a draft survives).
Cecilia's age (about 16) and the birth of her son Cesare in 1491, the year Ludovico married Beatrice d'Este: check.
Bellincioni's sonnet is paraphrased, not quoted.
Order of the Ermine awarded to Ludovico by the King of Naples in 1488, and the Greek pun (gale): standard readings.
Pascal Cotte's 2014 three-stage finding is his interpretation of the scans.
Black background being a later repaint over a blue-gray one, and the inscription being added in Poland around 1800: generally accepted; some recent studies question the repaint story.
Cecilia's 1498 letter to Isabella d'Este is paraphrased.
Hans Frank and the 1945 recovery in Bavaria: check.
Catalog year 1490; usually dated about 1489 to 1491.

lesson.text: Around 1489 Leonardo da Vinci was in his late thirties and, for once, on a salary. He had left Florence for Milan some seven years earlier, offering himself to its ruler, Ludovico Sforza, in a letter that boasted of bridges, cannons and siege machines. Painting came at the very end, almost as an afterthought.

Court life meant doing whatever the ruler wanted. Leonardo designed stage sets for parties, planned a colossal bronze horse that was never cast, and painted the people Ludovico cared about. One of them was Cecilia Gallerani, about sixteen, quick-witted, a writer of poems, and the ruler's mistress.
The timing was delicate. Ludovico was engaged to a duke's daughter, Beatrice d'Este, and married her in 1491. That same year Cecilia gave birth to his son. She was soon moved out of the castle.

A portrait of a mistress could not look like a portrait of a wife. Leonardo used the freedom to try something no Italian portrait had done. The girl does not simply sit and face one way. Her body tells you one thing and her head another.
Four directions in one small panel.

lines.label: The shoulders
lines.text: Her chest and shoulders are angled toward the left side of the picture. That is how she was sitting a moment ago.

lines.label: Her eyes
lines.text: Her head has swung the other way and her gaze passes out of the frame on the right. Something, or someone, has caught her attention.

lines.label: The animal
lines.text: The ermine turns its head on the same path, alert, ears up. Girl and animal react together.

lines.label: The light
lines.text: Light falls from the upper right, from the very direction she is looking, and leaves the back of her head in darkness.

lesson.text: So this is a picture of a reaction. A door has opened, a voice has spoken, and she turns. A court poet who knew the painting wrote that she seems to be listening and not speaking. Earlier portraits showed what a person looked like. This one shows a mind at work.
Leonardo's new idea here: a portrait can capture a thought. The twist of the body, a turn in the middle of a movement, became a tool for showing inner life.
And then there is the creature in her arms. It is too calm to be a pet and too large to be believed. To see why Leonardo put it there, look at how he built it.

lesson.title: The ermine
lesson.text: An ermine is a stoat in its white winter coat. This one has been improved.

spots.title: The head
spots.text: Small ears, a pink-rimmed eye, a blunt snout. Leonardo dissected animals and it shows. The skull under the fur feels solid.

spots.title: The raised paw
spots.text: One forepaw lifts and bends at the wrist, with each claw picked out. It is the pose of the heraldic beasts painted on coats of arms.

spots.title: Her hand
spots.text: Long fingers, every knuckle and tendon marked, rest on the animal's shoulder. The hand is oddly large, and it holds the ermine still without gripping it.

lesson.text: The animal carries at least three messages. Ermines stood for purity, because legend said they would rather die than dirty their white fur. The Greek word for the animal sounds like the start of Gallerani. And Ludovico himself had been awarded a knightly honor called the Order of the Ermine in 1488.

In 2014 an engineer who scanned the panel with special cameras reported that Leonardo changed his mind twice. First he painted Cecilia alone. Then he added a thin gray animal. Only at the end did it grow into the big white ermine.

A real ermine is under 30 cm long, about a foot. This one is the size of a small dog, with the shoulders of a hunting hound. The whole picture is only 54 by 39 cm (about 21 by 15 in), in oil on a walnut panel, so the animal fills a surprising share of it.

Not everything you see is by Leonardo. The background was once a lighter bluish gray and was later covered in flat black. And one corner carries a message from a later owner, who was wrong on two counts.
Someone wrote on this painting long after Leonardo died. Can you find the lettering?

spots.title: A mistaken label
spots.text: The faint capitals call her “La Bele Feroniere,” mixing her up with another portrait, and spell the painter's name “Leonard d'Awinci,” the Polish way. The label was added after the picture reached Poland.

lesson.text: It got there around 1800, when a Polish prince, Adam Jerzy Czartoryski, bought it in Italy as a gift for his mother, who was founding one of Poland's first museums. The family guarded it through uprisings and exile for more than a century.

In 1939 the Nazis seized the painting. It hung for a time in the Kraków office of Hans Frank, the Nazi governor of occupied Poland. Allied troops recovered it at his house in Bavaria in 1945, and it went home the next year.

Cecilia had her own last word on it. In 1498 a noblewoman asked to borrow the portrait. Cecilia sent it, with a warning that it no longer looked like her. The fault was not the master's, she explained. She had simply been so young when he painted it.

quiz.question: How did Leonardo present himself when he first offered his services in Milan?
quiz.explanation: His letter boasted of bridges, cannons and siege machines, with painting last.

quiz.question: Who was Cecilia Gallerani?
quiz.explanation: She was about sixteen and the ruler's mistress.

quiz.question: What was new about her pose?
options: She is shown in strict profile
Her body faces one way while her head turns the other
She looks straight at the viewer
quiz.explanation: The twist makes the portrait a picture of a reaction.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT a meaning of the ermine given in the lesson?
options: A reference to an honor held by Ludovico
A sign that Cecilia was a hunter
quiz.explanation: The lesson names purity, a pun on her name and Ludovico's Order of the Ermine.

quiz.question: What did scans in 2014 suggest?
options: The ermine was added and enlarged in stages
quiz.explanation: First no animal, then a thin gray one, then the large white ermine.

facts.text: The lettering in the top corner was written by Leonardo.
facts.explanation: It was added much later, after the painting reached Poland, and names the wrong sitter.

facts.text: The ermine is painted much larger than a real one.
facts.explanation: A real ermine is under 30 cm long, this one is the size of a small dog.

facts.text: The Nazis seized the painting during the Second World War.
facts.explanation: It was taken in 1939 and recovered in Bavaria in 1945.
